text: may be prevented by maintaining or slightly increasing plasma volume and blood pressure, and a fluid intake of 2 to 3 litres daily has been recommended.65 However, there is no good evidence to support routine volume expansion.69 Oral nimodipine is of benefit70 and should be started as soon as possible after diagnosis of subarachnoid haemor- rhage. Antiplatelet drugs have also been tried and may im- prove outcomes, but this remains to be confirmed.71 Estab- lished vasospasm may be treated by angioplasty, or intra- arterial vasodilators may be given. There is some evidence of benefit with intra-arterial papaverine,72 although ad- verse effects have also been reported;73 verapamil has also been used.74 Use of antifibrinolytics such as aminocaproic acid or tranexamic acid to prevent rebleeding is no longer generally recommended.65 A systematic review75 found that any benefits were offset by an increase in poor out- comes due to cerebral ischaemia; paradoxically, rebleed- ing has been noted in patients given high doses of amino- caproic acid after subarachnoid haemorrhage (see Effects on the Blood, under Adverse Effects of Aminocaproic Ac- id, p.1053). Headache can be managed with analgesics such as paracetamol, dextropropoxyphene, codeine, or tra- madol. Localised haematomas may be amenable to surgi- cal evacuation, and intraventricular thrombolytics have also been used.76 Intracerebral haemorrhage. Outcome of intracerebral haemorrhage depends on the location and size of the hae- matoma (determined by computed tomography), on the level of consciousness, and on the progression of neuro- logical signs, and development of increased intracranial pressure.77-79 Any known cause of bleeding, such as war- farin anticoagulation, should be reversed. Optimum man- agement of blood pressure is uncertain; it should probably be lowered when it is very high (>200 mmHg systolic80), but hypoperfusion should be avoided. Short-acting antihy- pertensives such as labetalol, esmolol, or sodium nitro- prusside are generally used,80 although theoretically nitro- prusside may increase intracranial pressure and should be avoided if this is already raised.79 Surgical drainage of the haematoma may sometimes be possible, but its role is uncertain;79,80 routine early surgery has not been shown81 to improve outcome. Instillation of a thrombolytic to im- prove aspiration of the haematoma has been reported,82 but benefit has not been established. Raised intracranial pressure should be controlled80 (see p.1181).
